results.message: How did someone become a Christian in your church?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
You are taught, then washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back to us, and then we baptize you. That is the ordinary shape. But a crowd at the door changes it. So the dying are not made to wait. The reconciliation he names there is the road back for someone who failed and is asking to return. That road is walked in stages, under the bishop, in the open. In our earliest years a confessor, Lucian, wrote from prison to another confessor, Celerinus: “And so, brother, I ask that it be done as it is here. When the Lord has begun to give peace to the Church itself, let each case be set before the bishop and the sin openly confessed. This is as Paulus commanded and as we ruled. Then let not only these women have peace, but also those whom you know to be dear to our heart.”

So even a confessor's own grant sent each case to the bishop.

glosses.plain_meaning: Discipline is the road; reconciliation is the arrival. What matters is that it is a road at all. There is an order to it, the order takes time, and everyone can see it.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, reconciliation is not a quiet, private pardon. It is a public road that a failed member walks, in stages, back into the community.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a brief private confession behind a screen, or a therapeutic notion of reconciliation -- repair achieved once both parties feel differently. Neither is private and neither is primarily about feeling for us. This is a public, staged, community-witnessed process with an examined entry, a real duration, and a formal act of readmission at the end, controlled by one office. What it restores is standing, and the whole community can see it being restored.
false_friend: a private sacramental confession, a few minutes long, said alone with no public witness
a therapeutic reconciliation between two parties, complete once both simply feel differently toward each other

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, a confessor is one who was interrogated for the Name, did not deny it, and lived. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop's own authority.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, a confessor is someone who was asked to deny the faith, did not, and lived. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener will almost certainly hear 'confessor' as a priest who hears confessions -- the later, Western, sacramental sense -- or a vague honorific for a saintly figure. We mean the opposite direction entirely: not one who hears confession, but one who made confession, under interrogation, at real risk, and survived. The word names what was done to us and what we did not say, and it carries a claim on the church's own decisions rather than an office within its ministry.
false_friend: a priest whose office is to hear other people's confessions, the later, Western, sacramental sense of the word
a vague honorific for any saintly figure, with no specific claim on church authority attached

confidence.divergence_note: Epistles XX-XXI are our own rare exception to the episcopal-voice monopoly -- two lay confessors, neither yet ordained, writing to each other in the first person (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). Even there the transaction itself is clerical and confessor-side; the reconciled believer does not speak anywhere in our record.

The evidence base for this term is essentially one Registry row (the Epistles) read through one lexicon entry, disclosed at generation rather than discovered afterwards (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). A phase bound was established by a check, not assumed: a sweep of all eight vendored Augustine volumes returns twenty occurrences of the stem against roughly 150 in Cyprian's one volume, and none carries this sense -- this term belongs to Cyprian's phase and does not cross into Augustine's.

The text field is the ANF English as printed. modern_rendering follows Hartel's Latin where the English misleads: cum Dominus coeperit is 'when the Lord has begun', not 'since'; facta exomologesi is the sin 'openly confessed'; tractatum, 'tractate', is the confessors' own ruling; hae and quas are feminine, 'these women' and 'those'; and '(all)' is the translator's supply, left out.
